title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal
subtitle: Compare larger machines with distributed capacity and their operational requirements
objectives: Distinguish scaling up from scaling out, and know which is a purchase and which is a redesign
Explain why vertical scaling runs out: ceiling, idle capacity, and single point of failure
Name what horizontal scaling demands in return — interchangeability and the cost of coordination
Choose deliberately: scale up until you have a reason not to, and know what that reason is

exercises.title: Vertical scaling enlarges one machine; horizontal scaling adds machines
exercises.body: *Vertical scaling* replaces or resizes a server to provide more CPU, memory, storage, or network capacity. *Horizontal scaling* runs additional server instances and partitions or distributes requests among them. Both increase capacity, while horizontal scaling changes how traffic and state are coordinated.
exercises.note: A horizontal tier requires a routing component and interchangeable instances, so request handling cannot depend on state stored only on one instance.

exercises.prompt: One application server handles 60 req/s while 90 req/s arrives. Add a second server and route traffic across both.
exercises.afterStatus: APPLICATION LOAD · 45 / 60 req/s on each server · 0 queued
exercises.why: A second interchangeable server adds processing capacity, while the load balancer makes that capacity reachable. This improves throughput and queueing only when the application can run correctly across multiple servers.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the system for this case: One application server handles 60 req/s while 90 req/s arrives. Add a second server and route traffic across both. Place Load balancer, Server A, Server B. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Users → Load balancer; Load balancer → Server A; Load balancer → Server B. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A second interchangeable server adds processing capacity, while the load balancer makes that capacity reachable. This improves throughput and queueing only when the application can run correctly across multiple servers.

exercises.prompt: Your server is at capacity. Option A: replace it with a machine that has 4× the CPU and RAM. Option B: run 4 copies of the machine you already have. What are these called?
choices: Upgrading and downgrading
Vertical scaling (scale up) and horizontal scaling (scale out)
Replication and sharding
Caching and load balancing
exercises.why: Vertical scaling increases the CPU, memory, or storage of one machine. Horizontal scaling adds machines and divides requests or work among them. Scaling up is usually an infrastructure change; scaling out also requires routing, interchangeable workers, and coordination for shared state.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to what it means.

pairs.right: The biggest machine money can buy
Capacity can grow by adding machines while work and dependencies can be partitioned

exercises.why: Vertical capacity stops at the largest available machine. A horizontal pool can accept additional machines, while useful capacity grows only when the workload can be partitioned and shared dependencies do not remain the bottleneck.

exercises.prompt: Buying a bigger machine is ______ scaling; running more machines is horizontal scaling.
choices: vertical
lateral
elastic
linear
exercises.why: Vertical scaling increases the resources of a single machine; horizontal scaling spreads the service across additional machines.

exercises.prompt: Which can you usually do today, with no code changes at all?
choices: Horizontal — just start more copies
Vertical — resize the box and your code neither knows nor cares
Neither — both need a rewrite
Both are equally easy
exercises.why: A vertical resize preserves the application's single-machine execution model. Capacity can often be increased through an instance-size change and a restart, with application code left unchanged. This is a practical first step when a larger machine is available and the restart fits the service's availability plan.

exercises.prompt: Your app runs on one server. You start a second copy. What has to be true for that to work?
choices: The servers must share their memory
Any request must be servable by either machine — so nothing a user needs can live only on one of them
They must have different code
The database must be replicated
exercises.why: A load balancer may send successive requests to different servers, so every eligible server must be able to obtain the session data, files, and other state needed to serve them. State held only on one server makes request routing dependent on that server and prevents full interchangeability.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are true of VERTICAL scaling? Select all.
choices: It's usually a config or hardware change, not a code change
It has a hard physical ceiling
It leaves you with a single point of failure
It requires your application to be stateless
exercises.why: Vertical scaling usually changes hardware or instance configuration, has a maximum machine size, and leaves the service dependent on one machine. It does not require a stateless application because requests continue to run on that same machine.

exercises.title: Vertical scaling selects a larger size from a finite instance family
exercises.body: A cloud instance family offers fixed CPU and memory sizes up to a largest machine. Within many mainstream families, on-demand price rises approximately in proportion to capacity. Resizing increases the resources of one failure domain and stops providing another step when the family maximum is reached.
exercises.note: A resize commonly requires a restart or replacement, and the enlarged machine still causes a full service outage if no redundant instance can take over.

exercises.prompt: A stateless API needs 240 request/s. One server handles 100 request/s and a larger machine is unavailable. Spread traffic across three equal servers.
exercises.afterStatus: CAPACITY · 300 request/s · about 80 request/s per server
exercises.result: Aggregate capacity exceeded demand with one server class
exercises.why: Horizontal scaling adds capacity by running interchangeable instances behind a distributor. It requires request state to be shared or externalized and creates coordination, deployment, and partial-failure work.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A stateless API needs 240 request/s. One server handles 100 request/s and a larger machine is unavailable. Spread traffic across three equal servers. Place Load balancer, 3 servers. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: 240 request/s → Load balancer; Load balancer → 3 servers. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Horizontal scaling adds capacity by running interchangeable instances behind a distributor. It requires request state to be shared or externalized and creates coordination, deployment, and partial-failure work.

exercises.prompt: Folklore says a machine with twice the cores costs more than twice as much. Is that true today?
choices: Yes — large machines are always disproportionately expensive
Mostly no: within a mainstream cloud instance family, price is close to linear — 2× the size costs about 2× the money
No — larger machines are always cheaper per core
It depends on the operating system
exercises.why: Within a mainstream cloud instance family, price generally rises close to linearly with virtual CPU and memory, so doubling resources often roughly doubles cost. The largest and specialized tiers can carry higher per-unit premiums. The economic crossover to horizontal scaling therefore depends on the workload, available instance tiers, and operational costs.

exercises.prompt: Match each limit of vertical scaling to what it means.

pairs.right: There is a biggest machine, and you can reach it
One box is sized for your peak, and idle the rest of the time
One machine dying means a total outage

exercises.why: The hard ceiling limits maximum capacity. Peak sizing leaves paid resources idle during quiet periods, a single machine remains one failure domain, and resizing commonly requires a restart. These constraints are independent, so vertical scaling can become operationally unsuitable before the size ceiling is reached.

exercises.prompt: You're already on the largest instance your cloud offers, and you're still at capacity. What are your vertical options?
choices: Wait for a bigger instance type
None — you've run out of road, and there's no incremental step left
Add more RAM to it
Restart it
exercises.why: Once the workload saturates the largest available instance, vertical scaling has no further capacity increment. Continuing growth then requires reducing the work or distributing it across machines, and that migration must be prepared before sustained load reaches the ceiling.

exercises.prompt: You have one very large machine serving everything. It dies. What's your availability?
choices: Unaffected — it's a big machine
Zero — you're down until it comes back or you rebuild
Degraded but fine
Depends on the CPU
exercises.why: A larger machine provides more capacity but remains a single failure domain. If it stops serving, no other machine can answer, so availability falls to zero until recovery or failover. Redundancy requires an independently operating copy of the service.

exercises.prompt: Resizing a machine to a larger instance usually requires what?
choices: Nothing — it's seamless and instant
A restart, so you need either a maintenance window or a failover to something else
A full data migration
Rewriting the application
exercises.why: Changing an instance's CPU or memory allocation commonly requires stopping and restarting it. A maintenance window accepts that interruption; a failover avoids user-visible downtime by routing traffic to another healthy machine during the resize.

exercises.prompt: Why does vertical scaling eventually stop being the answer? Select all.
choices: There is a largest machine, and you can reach it
One box can't shrink at 3am, so you pay for your peak around the clock
One machine is a single point of failure
It forces you to rewrite your application
exercises.why: Vertical scaling is bounded by the largest machine, keeps peak capacity allocated during low demand, and leaves one machine as a single point of failure. Application rewrites are not an inherent requirement of scaling up; avoiding them is one of its operational advantages.

exercises.title: Horizontal scaling requires work that can be distributed across instances
exercises.body: A load balancer may send consecutive requests to different instances. Each instance must therefore obtain required user state from a shared service or from the request itself. Work also needs independent partitions; operations that coordinate through one shared lock or record remain serialized.
exercises.note: A shared counter, lock, or database row can cap throughput for the whole tier even when unused CPU remains on individual instances.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Horizontal scaling requires work that can be distributed across instances
exercises.why: A load balancer may send consecutive requests to different instances. Each instance must therefore obtain required user state from a shared service or from the request itself. Work also needs independent partitions; operations that coordinate through one shared lock or record remain serialized. A shared counter, lock, or database row can cap throughput for the whole tier even when unused CPU remains on individual instances.

exercises.prompt: You add a second app server behind a load balancer. Immediately, users start getting randomly logged out. Why?
choices: The load balancer is misconfigured
Sessions live in one server's local memory, so requests landing on the other machine don't find them
The database can't handle two servers
The second server has old code
exercises.why: A session stored in server-local memory exists only on the server that created it. When the load balancer routes a later request to the other server, that server cannot find the session and treats the user as logged out. A shared session store or another explicit routing strategy is required.

exercises.prompt: Make two app servers interchangeable. Place the request distributor before the fleet and the session authority where either server can reach it.
exercises.why: The load balancer may send consecutive requests to either app server, so both must read the same session authority from a shared store. If sessions remain in local memory, a request routed to the other server cannot find the login; losing one server also loses every session stored only there.

exercises.prompt: You now run 3 identical app servers. Add the piece that spreads incoming traffic across them.
exercises.why: The load balancer accepts traffic at one service address and selects one of the three app servers for each request. This routing layer lets clients use the fleet without knowing individual server addresses or membership changes.

exercises.prompt: You split work across 10 machines, but every one of them must update the same shared counter. What happens?
choices: You get a 10× speedup
The shared counter becomes the bottleneck — you added machines, but the contended part didn't get any faster
The counter is automatically split
Nothing changes at all
exercises.why: Updates to one contended counter must be serialized or coordinated to preserve a correct value. All ten workers therefore queue at that shared resource, whose throughput bounds the system even though independent compute capacity increased.

exercises.prompt: Which workload scales horizontally most easily?
choices: One where every request must see the results of every other request
One where requests are independent of each other — like resizing uploaded images
One with a single shared lock
One that writes to the same row constantly
exercises.why: Each image resize can run from its own input and produce its own output without synchronizing with another resize. Independent tasks can be partitioned across workers, so added machines increase throughput with little coordination overhead.

exercises.prompt: So what does horizontal scaling actually demand in return?
choices: More expensive hardware
Interchangeable machines and work that can be split without constant coordination
A faster network only
Nothing — that's why it's better
exercises.why: Horizontal scaling requires eligible machines to be interchangeable for incoming requests and requires the workload to split without constant shared coordination. Server-local state violates interchangeability, while shared locks or counters can preserve a single throughput bottleneck.

exercises.title: Scaling strategy follows the measured constraint and availability target
exercises.body: Vertical scaling changes machine size with little application complexity until the size ceiling. Horizontal scaling adds routing, distributed state, partial failures, and multi-instance operations while enabling elastic capacity and redundancy. Choose the tier and resource that current measurements identify as constrained.
exercises.note: Capacity and availability are separate requirements: one machine may have enough CPU yet still violate an uptime target because its failure removes the entire service.

exercises.prompt: A startup with 5,000 users builds for horizontal scale from day one: six services, a message bus, the works. Likely outcome?
choices: They're ready for anything
They pay distributed-systems costs — coordination, partial failure, debugging across services — for a scale they don't have, and move slower than one box would have let them
It costs the same as one server
Their users notice the improvement
exercises.why: Six services and a message bus introduce network failure, cross-service observability, deployment coordination, and data-consistency work. With only 5,000 users, those recurring engineering costs may exceed the capacity benefit, while a simpler deployment can meet the measured load.

exercises.prompt: How far can a single modern machine actually take you?
choices: A few hundred users at most
Much further than most people assume — large servers can carry hundreds of cores and terabytes of RAM
Exactly one service
It depends only on the programming language
exercises.why: Large commodity and cloud machines can provide hundreds of CPU cores and terabytes of memory, so one machine may support substantial workloads when the application uses those resources effectively. The actual limit depends on request cost, storage access, concurrency, and the workload's measured bottleneck.

exercises.prompt: A small team runs one server at 900 peak req/s, 35% CPU, and 40% memory. Traffic is forecast to double over the next year, and its 99.5% uptime target permits planned maintenance. Choose the next-year capacity strategy.
exercises.why: Doubling the measured peak to 1,800 requests per second still leaves substantial CPU and memory headroom on one server, and the stated uptime target does not require redundancy. Scaling up or staying put for now avoids routing and partial-failure complexity; a stricter availability target or a measured single-machine bottleneck would shift the choice toward scaling out.

exercises.prompt: One machine has plenty of capacity for your traffic — but you need 99.99% uptime. Do you still need more machines?
choices: No — capacity is what matters
Yes — one machine is a single point of failure, and no amount of capacity fixes that
Only if traffic grows
Only during business hours
exercises.why: An idle machine can still fail, and a service with only that machine is unavailable during the failure. A 99.99% availability target therefore requires redundant serving capacity and failover even when traffic uses only a small fraction of one machine's capacity.

exercises.prompt: Which are genuine signals that it's time to scale out? Select all.
choices: You're approaching the largest machine available
Your uptime target requires redundancy
Traffic is spiky, and you want to add and remove capacity dynamically
Someone on the team read an article about microservices
exercises.why: Approaching the maximum machine size creates a capacity requirement; an uptime target creates a redundancy requirement; and large traffic swings create an elasticity requirement. A horizontally scaled pool can add or remove instances with demand, whereas architectural fashion provides no workload or reliability condition to justify the added complexity.

exercises.prompt: Your app servers are stateless and CPU-bound. Traffic doubles. Your database sits at 30% and is perfectly happy. What do you scale?
choices: The database — it's the important part
The app tier, horizontally — it's the bottleneck, and being stateless is exactly what makes that cheap
Everything, to be safe
Nothing — 30% is fine
exercises.why: The app tier is CPU-bound, while the database has spare capacity. Because app servers hold no request-specific local state, the load balancer can distribute requests across additional identical servers, increasing compute throughput at the active bottleneck.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of scaling?
choices: Distribute from day one — you'll need it eventually
Scale up first: it's simple, reversible, and goes further than people think. Scale out when you hit the ceiling, need redundancy, or need elasticity — knowing you're buying complexity
Never distribute; one machine is always enough
Whichever is cheaper this month
exercises.why: Scaling up is usually the simpler reversible step while a larger machine can satisfy capacity and availability requirements. Scaling out becomes appropriate when one machine approaches its ceiling, independent replicas are needed for availability, or capacity must track demand. It also introduces traffic distribution, state placement, and coordination requirements that must be designed explicitly.

exercises.prompt: A WebSocket process keeps each connected user's session only in local memory. Why can't a load balancer freely send the user's next message to any new server?
choices: WebSockets require one global CPU
The database must be NoSQL
The servers are not interchangeable for that session
Horizontal servers cannot use networks
exercises.why: Local connection state makes one process special. Horizontal routing needs connection-aware placement or shared/external state for operations that are allowed to move.
